B12C343.summary: Saunaka praises Sauti's recitation and asks why Narada went back to Vadari after seeing Narayana on White Island. Sauti explains that Janamejaya put the question to Vyasa during the snake sacrifice, and Vaisampayana then tells how Narada travels to Vadari and finds Nara and Narayana doing penance. Narada reports what he saw and decides to stay with the two sages. The chapter sets up the sages' teaching and frames the Narayana-centred devotion that the rest of the section develops.

scenes.B12C343S01: Saunaka's praise and question, Sauti's framing of Janamejaya's request, and Vaisampayana's account of Narada's journey to Vadari and his welcome by Nara and Narayana.
scenes.B12C343S02: Narada describes what he saw on White Island and says he has come back under the Lord's orders to live with Nara and Narayana.

shots.B12C343S01H01: Saunaka praises the story, says that talk of Narayana outweighs pilgrimages, and asks why Narada went back to Vadari after seeing Aniruddha.
shots.B12C343S01H02: Sauti says that Janamejaya, during his snake sacrifice, asked Vyasa the question that Saunaka has raised.
shots.B12C343S01H03: Janamejaya's question itself: what Narada did after White Island, how long he stayed at Vadari, and what the two sages said to him. He praises the Narayana teaching as drawn from the Bharata.
shots.B12C343S01H04: Vaisampayana begins the tale. Narada travels from White Island to Meru and Gandhamadana, reaches Vadari, and finds the two sages with their marks and penances. They welcome and honour him.
shots.B12C343S01H05: Nara and Narayana ask Narada whether he has seen the Supreme Soul on White Island.
shots.B12C343S02H01: Narada says he saw the immutable Being on White Island and sees the same marks in Nara and Narayana. He describes the devotion of the White Island folk, and says he came back under the Lord's orders to stay with them.

B12C344.summary: Nara and Narayana praise Narada for having seen Narayana and explain how the Supreme Soul is the source of the elements. They describe the path by which the liberated pass through successive forms into Vasudeva, and why they themselves took birth in Dharma's house. Narada becomes wholly devoted to Narayana and stays at Vadari for a thousand celestial years. The chapter gives the teaching that the rest of the section builds on.

scenes.B12C344S01: Nara and Narayana teach Narada about the Supreme Soul, the elements, and the path of the liberated, and Narada then settles into devotion and long residence at Vadari.

shots.B12C344S01H01: Nara and Narayana praise Narada for seeing Narayana and explain that the elements arise from the Lord, with each linked to a sense or quality. They describe the stages by which the liberated enter Vasudeva, and say they were born in Dharma's house to serve the Lord's future manifestations.
shots.B12C344S01H02: Vaisampayana says Narada joined his hands, devoted himself to Narayana, recited mantras, and stayed at Vadari for a thousand celestial years.

B12C345.summary: Nara asks Narada what rites he performs for the Pitris and why. Narada explains that he worships Vishnu through rites to the deities and Pitris, and recounts the old exchange of knowledge between sons and sires. Nara and Narayana then tell how Vishnu, as a boar, raised the Earth and made three mud balls as offerings, which became the Pitris, and why they are called Pindas. The chapter gives the origin story behind the Pinda offering, grounding it in Vishnu's act.

scenes.B12C345S01: Nara questions Narada about his rites, Narada explains his worship, and the two sages tell the origin of the Pitris and the Pinda offering.

shots.B12C345S01H01: Vaisampayana says that Narada, having finished the rites for the deities, begins the rites for the Pitris. Nara asks what he is worshipping and what he hopes to gain.
shots.B12C345S01H02: Narada replies that worship of the deities is the highest sacrifice and equal to worshipping the eternal Supreme Soul. He explains that Narayana is father, mother, and grandfather of all, and recalls how sons and sires once exchanged their knowledge of the Srutis and offered each other Pindas. He asks why the Pitris are called Pindas.
shots.B12C345S01H03: Nara and Narayana explain that the Earth was submerged and that Govinda, as a boar, raised her up. Afterwards Vishnu shook three balls of mud from his tusk, set them on grass, and offered them with sesame.
shots.B12C345S01H04: The god Vrishakapi, the same Vishnu in the story, declares that the three balls are the Pitris, and that he is their father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. He offers them with rites and then vanishes, which is why the Pitris are called Pindas. The passage closes by saying Narayana is the soul of all things.

B12C346.summary: Narada, after a thousand years with Nara and Narayana, returns to his own hermitage while the two sages stay on at Vadari. Vaisampayana then tells Janamejaya that hating Narayana brings ruin, that Vyasa is Narayana on earth, and urges him to carry on the horse sacrifice. Sauti reports that the king did so and ends with a long praise of Narayana as lord of the sages, refuge of the worlds, and slayer of demons. The chapter closes the Narada frame and returns the story to the sacrifice.

scenes.B12C346S01: Narada's departure, Vaisampayana's advice to the king to continue the horse sacrifice, and Sauti's account of the king's rites and a praise of Narayana.

shots.B12C346S01H01: Narada returns to his own retreat, and Vaisampayana tells Janamejaya that hating Narayana brings ruin, that Vyasa is Narayana on earth, and that the horse sacrifice should go on.
shots.B12C346S01H02: Sauti says the king carried out the sacrificial rites, notes that Narada first recited this teaching before a large audience including the Pandavas, Krishna, and Bhishma, and then praises Narayana at length.

B12C347.summary: Janamejaya asks why Hari took the horse-headed form that Brahma saw in the northern ocean, and what Brahma did afterwards. Vaisampayana tells how the world dissolves, how Brahma arises from Aniruddha, and how two demons seize the Vedas, leaving Brahma in grief. Narayana then takes the horse-headed form, recovers the Vedas, and slays the demons Madhu and Kaitabha, earning the name Madhusudana. The story closes by presenting Narayana as the source and soul of every quality and the refuge of both religions.

scenes.B12C347S01: Janamejaya's question, Sauti's framing, and Vaisampayana's account of the dissolution and creation, the theft of the Vedas, and Brahma's lament.
scenes.B12C347S02: Brahma's hymn to Narayana, the horse-headed form and recovery of the Vedas, the battle with the demons, and Vaisampayana's closing praise of this form.

shots.B12C347S01H01: Janamejaya recalls what he has heard about Narayana's births and the boar, and asks why the horse-headed form appeared in the northeastern ocean and what Brahma did after seeing it.
shots.B12C347S01H02: Sauti says he will tell the same old story that Vaisampayana once told at the snake sacrifice, since Janamejaya had asked the same question then.
shots.B12C347S01H03: Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana directly why Hari took the horse-headed form that Brahma saw on the northern shore.
shots.B12C347S01H04: Vaisampayana describes the world dissolving into primal Darkness, Brahma arising from Aniruddha to create, and two demons born from drops in the lotus seizing the Vedas and diving into the ocean.
shots.B12C347S01H05: Brahma laments that the Vedas are gone, asks who will restore them, and begins to praise Hari with joined hands.
shots.B12C347S02H01: Brahma praises Narayana, who then takes a horse-headed form, recovers the Vedas, and kills the demons Madhu and Kaitabha, earning the name Madhusudana.
shots.B12C347S02H02: Vaisampayana closes by calling this horse-headed form the oldest of Narayana's forms, says that reciting its story preserves learning, and presents Narayana as the source and refuge of the Vedas, Yoga, Sankhya, and all qualities.

B12C348.summary: Janamejaya asks who first taught the path of wholehearted devotion to Narayana, why it is said to surpass knowledge, and why most Brahmins follow other vows. Vaisampayana traces this teaching from Narayana through Brahma's many births and a long line of teachers, down to Narada, Vyasa, and Yudhishthira. He explains the three dispositions of Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas, says that the Sattwa type is closest to liberation through Narayana's grace, and concludes that the path is hard to practise. The chapter gives the doctrinal basis of devotion for the rest of the section.

scenes.B12C348S01: Janamejaya's questions about devotion, Vaisampayana's account of how the teaching was handed down, and his explanation of the three dispositions and who receives grace.
scenes.B12C348S02: Vaisampayana's closing summary: the path of renunciation of action, the unity of the teachings, and the warning that this doctrine is hard to practise.

shots.B12C348S01H01: Janamejaya says that Hari favours those devoted to him, that devotion may be superior to knowledge, and asks who first taught it, what its practices are, and when they began.
shots.B12C348S01H02: Vaisampayana says the teaching is hard to grasp, came from Narayana in the Krita age, and passed through Brahma's many births and a long line of Rishis and kings to Ikshaku, reaching the speaker through Narada and Vyasa.
shots.B12C348S01H03: Janamejaya asks why many learned Brahmins follow other vows and rites instead of this path.
shots.B12C348S01H04: Vaisampayana says people have three dispositions, that the Sattwa type is nearest to liberation, that liberation depends on Narayana, and that those of mixed or dull nature do not receive his favour.
shots.B12C348S01H05: Janamejaya asks how a being subject to change can reach the Supreme Purusha, and asks for the path of Pravritti to be explained in order.
shots.B12C348S02H01: Vaisampayana says the highest goal lies in giving up action, that the Sankhya, Aranyaka, and Pancharatra teachings form one whole, and that the teaching was passed to Yudhishthira through Narada and Vyasa. He ends by calling it hard to practise and naming Krishna as protector and destroyer of the universe.

B12C349.summary: Janamejaya asks whether the Sankhya, Pancharatra, and Aranyaka systems teach the same duties. Vaisampayana first honours Vyasa and then recounts Vyasa's own birth as he told it to his disciples: Narayana made Brahma, appointed a sage to arrange the Vedas, and foretold his own rebirth as Vyasa. Vaisampayana then surveys the main schools, all of which he says centre on Narayana, and begins Janamejaya's question of whether there are many Purushas or only one. The chapter sets up the dialogue between Brahma and Mahadeva that follows.

scenes.B12C349S01: Janamejaya's question about the systems, Vaisampayana's praise of Vyasa, and Vyasa's account of his birth from Narayana as told to his disciples.
scenes.B12C349S02: Vaisampayana's survey of the main cults, all centred on Narayana, and Janamejaya's question about one Purusha or many.
scenes.B12C349S03: Brahma and Mahadeva meet on Mount Vaijayanta, and Brahma explains which Purusha he meditates on.

shots.B12C349S01H01: Janamejaya asks whether the Sankhya, Pancharatra, and Aranyaka systems preach the same duties or different ones, and asks for an account of Pravritti.
shots.B12C349S01H02: Vaisampayana bows to Vyasa, son of Satyavati and Parasara, and calls him a portion of Narayana and the inexhaustible source of the Vedas.
shots.B12C349S01H03: Janamejaya asks how Vyasa, whose lineage he has already heard, could be a son of Narayana, and asks for the story of that birth.
shots.B12C349S01H04: Vaisampayana says that Vyasa, weary after composing the Mahabharata, was attended by his disciples on the Himalayas, and that they asked him to explain the Vedas and his own birth.
shots.B12C349S01H05: Vyasa tells his disciples that in the Krita age Narayana created Brahma, then took many forms to lighten the Earth, and appointed the sage Apantaratamas to arrange the Vedas, foretelling that he would be reborn as Vyasa. Vyasa adds that he is that same sage.
shots.B12C349S02H01: Vaisampayana names the founders of the Sankhya, Yoga, Pancharatra, Vedic, and Pasupata cults, and says that all of them treat Narayana as the one object of worship.
shots.B12C349S02H04: Janamejaya asks whether there are many Purushas or one, who is the foremost of them, and what is the source of all things.
shots.B12C349S02H05: Vaisampayana says the Sankhya and Yoga schools speak of many Purushas that share one origin in the Supreme Purusha. He then begins the tale of Brahma's discourse with Mahadeva on the mountain Vaijayanta.
shots.B12C349S03H01: Brahma welcomes his son Mahadeva after a long absence and asks about his penances and his study of the Vedas.
shots.B12C349S03H02: Mahadeva says all is well and asks why Brahma has withdrawn to a lonely mountain away from his heavenly home.
shots.B12C349S03H03: Brahma says that he has made Vaijayanta his home and meditates there on the one universal Purusha.
shots.B12C349S03H04: Mahadeva notes that many Purushas have been created and asks which Purusha Brahma is meditating on.
shots.B12C349S03H05: Brahma answers that the many Purushas rest on one Purusha, who is beyond all attributes, and that those who shed their attributes can enter into him.

B12C350.summary: Brahma tells Mahadeva what the one Purusha is like: eternal, beyond the reach of anyone without self-control, present in every body, and called Kshetrajna. Brahma explains that this Purusha is Narayana, the Supreme Soul, and that the universe and its many souls come from him in the fourfold form of Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Sankarshana, and Vasudeva. He adds that Brahma himself arose from this Purusha, and that the Sankhya and Yoga teachings agree with this account. The chapter states the chapter's central doctrine of a single, all-pervading Purusha.

scenes.B12C350S01: Brahma's full answer to Mahadeva about the one Purusha, his nature, his manifestation as Narayana, and the origin of everything from him.

shots.B12C350S01H01: Brahma describes the one Purusha as eternal, unseen by the undisciplined, present in all bodies, and known as Kshetrajna, then explains that he is Narayana, the Supreme Soul, in the fourfold form, and that Brahma himself and all the Vedas come from him.

B12C351.summary: Vaisampayana turns to a new topic: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which duties are foremost for each stage of life. Bhishma replies that duties can all lead to heaven if performed faithfully. He then says he will repeat a story that Narada once told Indra, which sets up the teaching that follows. The chapter is a short introduction to a new frame story about how to choose one's duty.

scenes.B12C351S01: Sauti's introduction, Yudhishthira's question to Bhishma about the foremost duties of each stage of life, and Bhishma's answer that he will recount Narada's talk with Indra.

shots.B12C351S01H01: Sauti says Vaisampayana, after praising Narayana to Janamejaya, now recounts Yudhishthira's question to Bhishma in the presence of the Pandavas, the Rishis, and Krishna.
shots.B12C351S01H02: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to say which duties are foremost for persons in each mode of life, having already heard about the religion of liberation.
shots.B12C351S01H03: Bhishma says every duty can lead to heaven if performed well, then says this question was once discussed by Narada and Indra, and that he will repeat that story.

B12C352.summary: Bhishma tells of a Brahmin householder in the city of Mahapadma who has many children and wealth, but is troubled about which of three kinds of duty to follow. When a learned guest visits, the host confesses that he wants to hand his household to his son and seek liberation, yet cannot give up his attachments. The guest admits he is equally confused and lists the many routes to heaven that people follow. The chapter sets the puzzle that the rest of the story will try to resolve.

scenes.B12C352S01: Bhishma introduces a householder's doubts about duty, his conversation with a guest about renunciation, and the guest's reply that many paths lead to heaven.

shots.B12C352S01H01: Bhishma describes a learned, virtuous Brahmin of Atri's line in the city of Mahapadma, with a large family, who is troubled about which of three kinds of duty to follow, and who then receives a guest.
shots.B12C352S01H02: The host tells the guest he wants to give his household to his son and seek liberation, but is held back by attachment, and he asks what path he should take.
shots.B12C352S01H03: Bhishma says the guest, a wise Brahmin, answered the host in a gentle voice.
shots.B12C352S01H04: The guest says he is equally confused and lists many routes to heaven, including renunciation, sacrifice, study, truth, and battle, concluding that his own understanding has been clouded by the question.

B12C353.summary: The guest offers to guide the host, though he says the question is hard. He points him to a wise Naga named Padmanabha who lives in a city in the Naimisha forest on the Gomati, and he describes the Naga's many virtues. The host is directed toward a teacher he can trust. The chapter moves the search to a new teacher.

scenes.B12C353S01: The guest's instruction, naming the Naga Padmanabha in Naimisha and describing his character.

shots.B12C353S01H01: The guest says he will still try to instruct the host, names the Naga Padmanabha in a city of Nagas in the Naimisha forest by the Gomati, and lists his many virtues as a guide who is generous, learned, and fair.

B12C354.summary: The host is deeply relieved by the guest's words and says he now knows what to do. The two spend the night in talk about renunciation, and the night passes quickly. In the morning the host honours the guest, takes leave of his family, and sets out for the Naga's dwelling.

scenes.B12C354S01: The host's gratitude, the night spent in talk about renunciation, and the host's departure the next morning.

shots.B12C354S01H01: The host says he feels as relieved as a weary traveller or a thirsty man who finds water, promises to act on the guest's advice, and invites him to rest for the night.
shots.B12C354S01H02: Bhishma says the two talk through the night about renunciation, and in the morning the host sends his guest off and sets out for the Naga's home with his mind fixed on it.

B12C355.summary: The Brahmin reaches the Naga's house and announces himself as a guest. The Naga's devoted wife welcomes him and explains that her husband is away for a month, pulling the Sun's chariot, and will return in fifteen days. The Brahmin says he will wait on the bank of the Gomati and asks her to tell the Naga he has come.

scenes.B12C355S01: The Brahmin's arrival at the Naga's house, his request to see the Naga, the wife's reply about her husband's absence, and his decision to wait by the Gomati.

shots.B12C355S01H01: The Brahmin travels through forests and holy waters, asks an ascetic about the Naga, and arrives at the Naga's house, where the Naga's chaste wife greets him as a guest.
shots.B12C355S01H02: The Brahmin says he is well received and has come only to see her husband.
shots.B12C355S01H03: The wife explains that her husband is pulling the Sun's car for a month and will be back in fifteen days, and offers to help in other ways.
shots.B12C355S01H04: The Brahmin says he will wait on the bank of the Gomati, living on simple food, and asks her to tell the Naga he has come, which he repeats.

B12C356.summary: The Naga's kinsmen are alarmed to see the Brahmin fasting by the Gomati, and they plead with him to eat, arguing that his fast shames their hospitality. The Brahmin says he will only break his fast after the Naga returns, and he asks them to go home. The chapter shows the guest's vow standing firm and the household's concern.

scenes.B12C356S01: The Naga's relatives plead with the fasting Brahmin, and he refuses, sending them home.

shots.B12C356S01H01: Bhishma says the Naga's relatives, including his brother, children, and wife, come to the Brahmin on the Gomati, see him fasting and reciting mantras, and beg him to eat, saying his fast reflects badly on them.
shots.B12C356S01H02: The Brahmin says he will break his fast after eight more days, if the Naga is still away, and asks the relatives to go home and not to disturb his vow.

B12C357.summary: The Naga returns home after fifteen days, washes his feet, and asks his wife whether she kept up worship and hospitality in his absence. She explains the duties of each class and of the householder, then reports that a Brahmin has been waiting by the Gomati for many days. She urges her husband to go and grant the guest's request.

scenes.B12C357S01: The Naga's return, his questions to his wife about his household duties, and her reply on the duties of each class and her appeal that he meet the waiting Brahmin.

shots.B12C357S01H01: Bhishma says the Naga comes home after finishing his work for the Sun, and asks his wife whether she has kept up the worship of gods and guests and remained virtuous in his absence.
shots.B12C357S01H02: The wife says she has kept her duties, lists the duties of disciples, Brahmins, servants, kings, Kshatriyas, Sudras, and householders, and reports that the Brahmin is waiting by the Gomati, urging the Naga to go to him.

B12C358.summary: The Naga asks whether the Brahmin is a human or a god, since few humans would seek him out. His wife argues that the guest is sincere and that a man of standing must not turn away a needy visitor. The Naga admits he has been moved by her teaching, cites the ruin that wrath brought to Ravana and to Kartavirya's sons, and agrees to go and meet the Brahmin.

scenes.B12C358S01: The Naga questions whether the guest is human, his wife urges him to attend to the guest, and the Naga agrees to meet him after a reflection on the harm of wrath.

shots.B12C358S01H01: The Naga asks his wife whether the Brahmin could be a god in disguise, since humans seldom seek out the Nagas, and says Nagas are hard for humans to see.
shots.B12C358S01H02: The wife says the guest is not a god who lives on air, that he sincerely reveres her husband, and that a man must not turn a guest away. She lists the merits of generosity, truth, and duty, and urges him to see the Brahmin.
shots.B12C358S01H03: The Naga says her words have calmed his wrath, cites Ravana, the sons of Kartavirya, and Kartavirya himself as examples of wrath's downfall, and resolves to go and speak with the Brahmin.

B12C359.summary: The Naga goes out to the waiting Brahmin, wondering what has brought him, and greets him with courtesy. The Brahmin gives his name as Dharmaranya and explains that he has come to see Padmanabha on business, reciting the Vedas and practising yoga while he waits. The Naga identifies himself and offers to help in any way, and the Brahmin says he will reveal his request after first asking a question. The chapter opens the direct meeting between the two.

scenes.B12C359S01: The Naga meets the Brahmin on the Gomati, the Brahmin introduces himself and his purpose, and the Naga offers his service.

shots.B12C359S01H01: Bhishma says the Naga goes to the waiting Brahmin, wondering what business brought him, and greets him kindly, asking whom he worships in this quiet spot.
shots.B12C359S01H02: The Brahmin, named Dharmaranya, says he came to see the Naga Padmanabha on some business, and has been reciting the Vedas and practising yoga while he waits.
shots.B12C359S01H03: The Naga says he is the Naga the Brahmin seeks, praises his conduct, and offers to do whatever is asked of him, since the Brahmin's merit has bound them to him.
shots.B12C359S01H04: The Brahmin says he seeks to reach the Supreme Soul through the individual soul, and asks the Naga first to answer a question about the wonders he has seen before he states his request.

B12C360.summary: The Brahmin asks the Naga, who pulls the Sun's chariot in turns, to describe any wonder he has seen on his journeys. The Naga praises the Sun as the source of creatures and of the rains, and the dwelling place of the Supreme Soul. He then describes a radiant being who approached the Sun at noon and merged into it, so that the Nagas could no longer tell the two apart.

scenes.B12C360S01: The Brahmin's request for a marvel, the Naga's account of the Sun's wonders, and his description of the radiant being who joined the Sun.

shots.B12C360S01H01: The Brahmin asks the Naga, who pulls the Sun's car in turn, to describe any wonder he has seen on his journeys.
shots.B12C360S01H02: The Naga describes the Sun's wonders, including the wind, the rains, and the Soul said to dwell in the solar disc, then tells of a shining being that approached the Sun at noon and merged into him, leaving the Nagas unable to say which was which.

B12C361.summary: Surya himself explains who the radiant being was: a Brahmin who reached heaven through the Unccha vow, living on fruit, roots, fallen leaves, water, or air, and devoted to Mahadeva. The Naga reports this explanation, adding that the Brahmin now travels round the Earth from within the Sun's disc. The chapter closes the Naga's story of the wonder and answers the Brahmin's question.

scenes.B12C361S01: Surya's explanation of the radiant being as a Brahmin who attained heaven through the Unccha vow, with the Naga's concluding remarks.

shots.B12C361S01H01: Surya explains that the being is neither a god, an Asura, nor a Naga, but a Brahmin who reached the Sun's disc through the Unccha vow and devotion to Mahadeva, and who still circles the Earth from there.
shots.B12C361S01H02: Editor's note: there was no section CCLXIV in the source edition.

B12C362.summary: Dharmaranya leaves the Naga, having learned from him that the Unccha vow, living by gleaning, is the right path to take. He goes to the sage Chyavana to be formally initiated into it. Bhishma traces the teaching back through Janaka, Narada, Indra, and the Vasus, and says it answers Yudhishthira's question about the highest duty. The main text ends with the close of the Santi Parva, and the rest of the chapter is a long run of translator's footnotes that explain Sanskrit words, variant readings, and difficult passages.

scenes.B12C362S01: The Brahmin's farewell to the Naga, his resolve to live by the Unccha vow, his initiation by Chyavana, and the chain of teachers through whom the story reached Bhishma.
scenes.B12C362S02: Translator's notes 1 to 4, on the period of impurity after a death, a phrase about inward light, and the weapon that will not come back at death.
scenes.B12C362S03: Translator's notes 5 to 9, on variant readings, Yudhishthira's argument about the slain warriors, pairs of opposites, and why wealth matters for rites.
scenes.B12C362S04: Translator's notes 10 to 14, on the forest recluses who gather fallen fruit, the origin of one's possessions, and a gloss on one word.
scenes.B12C362S05: Translator's notes 15 to 19, on the Ordainer and the duties of Kshatriyas, the merit of sacrifice, and the fate of souls after death.
scenes.B12C362S06: Translator's notes 20 to 24, on the gods' rise through action, the word for non-believer, the path of the gods, and the false renouncer.
scenes.B12C362S07: Translator's notes 25 to 29, on whether Yudhishthira should rule, the threefold aims of life, and the body as a meaning of mind.
scenes.B12C362S08: Translator's notes 30 to 34, on selfish action leading to death, a variant reading, the three kinds of strength, and the graded punishments for each class.
scenes.B12C362S09: Translator's notes 35 to 39, on the fisherman's livelihood, killing to live, the sense of a boundary word, fear as a force, and the rod for the child.
scenes.B12C362S10: Translator's notes 40 to 44, on killing a tiger to protect the herd, the three humours, Arjuna's wrath at his wife's insult, and the cost of abandoning prosperity.
scenes.B12C362S11: Translator's notes 45 to 49, on conquering the mind, the restored locks of Draupadi, the tiger as a fisher, the penances of kings, and the desire that remains.
scenes.B12C362S12: Translator's notes 50 to 54, on false renunciation in luxury, the paths of the Pitris and the gods, the unity of all beings, and sacrifice.
scenes.B12C362S13: Translator's notes 55 to 59, on dependence on destiny, the wife as a partner in acts, the case of Janaka, and the fire for libations.
scenes.B12C362S14: Translator's notes 60 to 64, on Janaka resuming his kingdom, ruling without attachment, the Nyaya view of the soul, and ignorance as the cause of rebirth.

shots.B12C362S01H01: The Brahmin thanks the Naga for his teaching, says he is satisfied, and asks to be remembered and sent for now and then.
shots.B12C362S01H02: The Naga asks what business brought the Brahmin, says he should stay, since he and the Brahmin are now friends.
shots.B12C362S01H03: The Brahmin agrees that the Naga is equal to the gods in wisdom, says his doubt is resolved through the Unccha vow, and takes his leave.
shots.B12C362S01H04: Bhishma says the Brahmin went to the sage Chyavana to be initiated into the Unccha life, and traces the story through Janaka, Narada, Indra, and the Vasus to himself.
shots.B12C362S01H05: Closing line: the end of the Santi Parva.
shots.B12C362S02H02: Note 1: a period of impurity after a death, which the Sraddha rite ends.
shots.B12C362S02H03: Note 2: the phrase literally means the thing will not appear by inward light.
shots.B12C362S02H04: Note 3: the weapon will leave the man's memory near death, though he may command it at other times.
shots.B12C362S02H05: Note 4: the Kurus who fell in battle have gone to heaven, and grief is now the lot of the living.
shots.B12C362S03H01: Note 5: the reading Sanjata Valaratnesu is the true one.
shots.B12C362S03H02: Note 6: the Bombay reading Jayaphalam is correct, though the Bengal reading is not meaningless.
shots.B12C362S03H03: Note 7: Yudhishthira argues that the slain warriors did not reach heaven, since men of wrath cannot.
shots.B12C362S03H04: Note 8: pairs of opposites such as heat and cold, joy and grief.
shots.B12C362S03H05: Note 9: wealth lets its owner perform religious rites.
shots.B12C362S04H01: Note 10: if one does not wrong forest dwellers, there is less chance of wronging townsmen.
shots.B12C362S04H02: Note 11: recluses who take fallen fruit as the tree's alms, treating the tree as a guest.
shots.B12C362S04H03: Note 12: possessions and kinsfolk depend on past acts, and also shape later lives.
shots.B12C362S04H04: Note 13: those for whom one acts do not take on the results of one's acts.
shots.B12C362S04H05: Note 14: Nilakantha's gloss on one word, as the lordship of heaven.
shots.B12C362S05H01: Note 15: since the Ordainer cannot be blamed, the duties he gave Kshatriyas cannot be blamed either.
shots.B12C362S05H02: Note 16: those who sacrifice and eat the offering acquire merit no other act can match.
shots.B12C362S05H03: Note 17: a grammar note; one who firmly regards himself as Siva gains success like that deity's, as the Srutis say.
shots.B12C362S05H04: Note 18: those who die in the bright fortnight of summer reach the sun, those in the dark fortnight of winter the moon, and the detached reach Brahma's realm.
shots.B12C362S05H05: Note 19: without gods, Pitris, or Brahma, souls sink and become worms and vermin.
shots.B12C362S06H01: Note 20: the gods themselves became gods through action.
shots.B12C362S06H02: Note 21: the first word is a compound of a negative and the word for believer.
shots.B12C362S06H03: Note 22: the path of the gods is the strict observance of the Vedic rites.
shots.B12C362S06H04: Note 23: the renouncer is one who wastes his body by fasting, so in effect he denies himself.
shots.B12C362S06H05: Note 24: such a person is not a true renouncer, and for a Kshatriya such a life would be sinful.
shots.B12C362S07H01: Note 25: Nilakantha says this life suits a Brahmin, not a Kshatriya, so Yudhishthira would sin by leaving the rule to a brother.
shots.B12C362S07H02: Note 26: acts done from vanity, claiming to be the doer, differ from acts done in renunciation, without hope of fruit.
shots.B12C362S07H03: Note 27: the threefold aims of life are religion, pleasure, and profit.
shots.B12C362S07H04: Note 28: Nilakantha's explanation of the word antarala.
shots.B12C362S07H05: Note 29: the word for the inner self is set against the outer, and explained as encased in the body, that is the mind.
shots.B12C362S08H01: Note 30: Sahadeva's point is that selfish action brings death, while the opposite attitude leads to Brahma.
shots.B12C362S08H02: Note 31: the sense depends on one word, and a variant would leave the sense unchanged.
shots.B12C362S08H03: Note 32: the three kinds of strength are the master's power, good counsel, and one's own courage and perseverance.
shots.B12C362S08H04: Note 33: a literal rendering: crushed with the rod of chastisement.
shots.B12C362S08H05: Note 34: punishments by class: censure for a Brahmin, loss of property for a Kshatriya, forfeiture for a Vaisya, and little or none for a Sudra.
shots.B12C362S09H01: Note 35: a fisherman who would not kill fish would go without food.
shots.B12C362S09H02: Note 36: killing these creatures to support life is no sin.
shots.B12C362S09H03: Note 37: Nilakantha glosses the word for enjoyment as a boundary or limit.
shots.B12C362S09H04: Note 38: the cow gives milk, and maidens marry, only out of fear of punishment.
shots.B12C362S09H05: Note 39: fear of being thought a fool induces a learner to study, though it is not as harsh as the saying about the rod.
shots.B12C362S10H01: Note 40: killing a tiger that attacks the herd is better than standing by, since passive witnessing is itself a sin.
shots.B12C362S10H02: Note 41: the three humours are phlegm, bile, and wind.
shots.B12C362S10H03: Note 42: the speaker was always above joy and grief, and never swayed by either.
shots.B12C362S10H04: Note 43: the argument is that the insult to his wife should stir Arjuna's wrath, which justifies the slaying of his foes.
shots.B12C362S10H05: Note 44: having given up prosperity and kingship, Yudhishthira must be reborn and fight his doubts again.
shots.B12C362S11H01: Note 45: a difficult verse, which Nilakantha reads as a call to conquer the mind, the foe of the unmanifest self.
shots.B12C362S11H02: Note 46: Draupadi's locks, which were unbound after Duhsasana seized her, are restored after the slaughter.
shots.B12C362S11H03: Note 47: the Bengal tiger acts as a fisher, and the translator has seen its catch with claw-marks sold in a village market.
shots.B12C362S11H04: Note 48: kings cannot escape hell without penances, which are hard to perform amid luxury, so taking wealth and not using it is impractical.
shots.B12C362S11H05: Note 49: a sign that one is not free from desire.
shots.B12C362S12H01: Note 50: false speech here means claiming detachment while enjoying wealth and power.
shots.B12C362S12H02: Note 51: the path of the Pitris is Vedic ritual for future bliss, and the path of the gods is contemplation without rites.
shots.B12C362S12H03: Note 52: unity with the Supreme Soul is attaining Brahma, and selfishness, the root of sin, then disappears.
shots.B12C362S12H04: Note 53: the word refers to sacrifice.
shots.B12C362S12H05: Note 54: a literal rendering: your resolve is of one kind, while your acts are of another.
shots.B12C362S13H01: Note 55: Nilakantha reads the word as dependent on destiny, though the simpler sense is dependent on action.
shots.B12C362S13H02: Note 56: a wedded wife is a companion in one's religious acts.
shots.B12C362S13H03: Note 57: one should therefore not give up action.
shots.B12C362S13H04: Note 58: a true renouncer stands alone, so Janaka's giving up wife and kingdom does not fit perfect renunciation, and he could have enjoyed them without attachment.
shots.B12C362S13H05: Note 59: such libations work only when poured on fires kindled with mantras.
shots.B12C362S14H01: Note 60: Janaka should resume his kingdom and give alms, or else mendicants would be ruined.
shots.B12C362S14H02: Note 61: a man could rule a kingdom and still be a mendicant, if he rules without attachment.
shots.B12C362S14H03: Note 62: refers to the Nyaya definition of the soul by desire, aversion, will, pleasure, pain, and the faculties of knowing.
shots.B12C362S14H04: Note 63: the soul, though without attributes, passes from body to body through ignorance, and once freed from ignorance it ceases to act.
shots.B12C362S14H05: Note 64: the three phrases mean learned in reasoning, firmly convinced from a past life, and hard to understand.
shots.B12C362S15H01: Note 65: it is better to give up sacrifices that cannot be done without wealth.
shots.B12C362S15H02: Note 66: the word for self here means wealth, and misusing wealth is a kind of killing of oneself and a sin like killing a foetus.
shots.B12C362S15H03: Note 67: the Srutis say that whoever frightens others is frightened himself, so Yudhishthira is urged to take the throne.
shots.B12C362S15H04: Note 68: Nilakantha's reading of a phrase, meaning that some do praise contemplation.
shots.B12C362S15H05: Note 69: a literal rendering: lack of contentment with present prosperity.
shots.B12C362S16H01: Note 70: the word means a robber who takes property by force, and some texts read a different word.
shots.B12C362S16H02: Note 71: Manu also gives the king a sixth of the produce.
shots.B12C362S16H03: Note 72: Nilakantha explains the word as meaning one without pride.
shots.B12C362S16H04: Note 73: yoga here means vigour in action, and nyasa means giving up pride.
shots.B12C362S16H05: Note 74: those who by dying have escaped all grief.
shots.B12C362S17H01: Note 75: Nilakantha glosses one word as meaning increased.
shots.B12C362S17H02: Note 76: true knowledge is knowledge of Brahma, and conduct should follow the view of those who have it.
shots.B12C362S17H03: Note 77: it is better not to covet wealth for sacrifice, and a poor man does better to skip sacrifice than to use ill-gotten wealth.
shots.B12C362S17H04: Note 78: the speaker undertakes severe penance so as not to be reborn as a lower animal.
shots.B12C362S17H05: Note 79: 'even such' means arising from such causes.

shots.B12C362S26H04: Note 123: the priest of the Kauravas.

shots.B12C362S29H03: Note 137: the Supreme Being is called Hansa, the swan, and That, as in the Vedic formula, beyond words.
shots.B12C362S29H04: Note 138: Brahma has no attributes we can name.
shots.B12C362S29H05: Note 139: the Vaks are mantras, the Anuvaks are Brahmanas, the Nishads lead to knowledge of the gods, and the Upanishads deal with knowledge of the Soul.

shots.B12C362S30H04: Note 143: these are the twelve Adityas, the chief gods.

shots.B12C362S31H03: Note 147: sandhis are euphonic changes between vowels, and akshara means a letter.
shots.B12C362S31H04: Note 148: the manifest is the body, the field is intelligence, and the Supreme Being is called Kshetrajna because he knows every mind.

shots.B12C362S32H04: Note 153: the word means a Brahmacharin, a celibate student.

shots.B12C362S33H03: Note 157: the Vedas are the speech of the Supreme Being, and all morality is found in them.
shots.B12C362S33H04: Note 158: a literal rendering: everything you know will appear to you by inward light.
shots.B12C362S33H05: Note 159: the speaker already has full fame and can scarcely add to it.
shots.B12C362S34H01: Note 160: a literal rendering: the eternal bridge of virtue.

shots.B12C362S34H03: Note 162: literally, worthy of being used by the king.

shots.B12C362S36H04: Note 173: the phrase means rose above the five, that is renounced the world, not died as the earlier version had it.
shots.B12C362S36H05: Note 174: a Manwantara is a very long period of time, comparable to a geological age.

shots.B12C362S38H01: Note 180: the phrase means returning unwounded from battle.
shots.B12C362S38H02: Note 181: without battle a king cannot extend his kingdom and gain wealth for gifts and sacrifices.

shots.B12C362S38H05: Note 184: the word atirekena means with excessive zeal, not with a surplus.

shots.B12C362S41H03: Note 197: the services of such people should not be taken as priests.

shots.B12C362S42H02: Note 201: the rules have exceptions and limits.

shots.B12C362S51H05: Note 249: trees such as banian and peepul give shade to travellers.

shots.B12C362S110H04: Note 543: dattam covers protecting suppliants, not injuring creatures, and gifts outside the altar, and ishta covers keeping the sacred fire, penance, study, hospitality, and offerings.
shots.B12C362S110H05: Note 544: even if he seeks to avoid it.
shots.B12C362S111H01: Note 545: the phrase means becomes his inseparable associate.
shots.B12C362S111H02: Note 546: when past acts are exhausted, the creature is freed, but orthodox Hindus hold that some balance always remains, so a new birth follows.
shots.B12C362S111H03: Note 547: samunnam means drenched in water, and upavasah here means giving up all possessions, though it usually means fasting.
shots.B12C362S111H04: Note 548: the phrase that the track of the virtuous cannot be marked probably means they leave no record, having given up all action.
shots.B12C362S111H05: Note 549: manasa means of the mind, or the will, and mahat means great.
shots.B12C362S112H01: Note 550: Veda here means knowledge and power.
shots.B12C362S112H02: Note 551: Nilakantha explains the compound as the one who is the soul of all beings, and cites the Srutis on the five elements.
shots.B12C362S112H03: Note 552: the word devah means luminous or shining ones here, not gods.
shots.B12C362S112H04: Note 553: the Rishis thought that pouring water created air, instead of merely showing it.
shots.B12C362S112H05: Note 554: all created things are bhutas, but the five principal elements are called Mahabhutas.
shots.B12C362S113H01: Note 555: this shows the ancient Hindus knew how to treat diseased plants and restore them.
shots.B12C362S113H02: Note 556: K.P. Singha misrenders this verse, and the Burdwan translator is right.
shots.B12C362S113H03: Note 557: the Bengal and Bombay texts read bhutani, but the correct reading seems to be bhutanam.
shots.B12C362S113H04: Note 558: the word for duct is srotas, also rendered channel, which is like the main artery or aorta.
shots.B12C362S113H05: Note 559: despite crude anatomy and physiology, the Rishis glimpsed some truths, and verse 15 anticipates Harvey's discovery of circulation.
shots.B12C362S114H01: Note 560: yoga teaches that the main duct should be brought under the will, so the soul is withdrawn into the brain and the creature is freed from food and sleep.
shots.B12C362S114H02: Note 561: in an advanced stage of yoga the Soul is said to behold itself, which the translator takes as figurative.
shots.B12C362S114H03: Note 562: the commentator says the four classes match the attributes of Goodness, Passion, a mixture of both, and Darkness.
shots.B12C362S114H04: Note 563: the eternal creation is due to the Deity's yoga, while the visible creation is due to the penances of the first sages.
shots.B12C362S114H05: Note 564: the word ghrina may also mean aversion, here aversion to unrighteous acts.
shots.B12C362S115H01: Note 565: the Bombay reading of the first half of verse 6 is clearer, though the Bengal reading is kept, and the verb means one who acquires fame.
shots.B12C362S115H02: Note 566: the speaker describes renunciation of acts, with sacrifices and rites in view, and the second line could mean one who pours everything out in gifts.
shots.B12C362S115H03: Note 567: behind the gross world is a subtle one, and after death the subtle body, the linga-sarira, remains until absorption into Brahma.
shots.B12C362S115H04: Note 568: heaven's felicity is not everlasting and lasts only as long as the merit earned on earth.
shots.B12C362S115H05: Note 569: the Puranic theory of eclipses holds that the Daitya Rahu seeks to devour the Sun and Moon.
shots.B12C362S116H01: Note 570: the Vedas declare these fruits so that men may strive for what leads to happiness.
shots.B12C362S116H02: Note 571: nearly the whole of this section is prose.
shots.B12C362S116H03: Note 572: the translator finds it hard to tell in what senses Dharma is used in the three questions.
shots.B12C362S116H04: Note 573: the correct reading in the first line is brahmana, not brahmarshi, as the answer ascribed to Bhrigu shows.
shots.B12C362S116H05: Note 574: a pupil should wait to be called by his teacher and never ask for instruction, and the translator gives an anecdote of a teacher who went on teaching after a son's death.
shots.B12C362S117H01: Note 575: the phrase means picking up fallen grains from a field after the crop has been removed.
shots.B12C362S117H03: Note 577: by procreating, one gratifies the Creator, the same idea behind the command to multiply, with a parallel in Jewish law.
shots.B12C362S117H04: Note 578: the end of these attributes is Moksha, or liberation.
shots.B12C362S117H05: Note 579: sishta means one properly instructed by wise preceptors.
shots.B12C362S118H01: Note 580: niyama is a rite, upayoga is a vow about food, charyya is an act such as visiting sacred waters, and vihita is vidhana.
shots.B12C362S118H02: Note 581: the Hindus had no poor laws, since scripture supported the poor and mendicants, and mendicants called only on the well-to-do.
shots.B12C362S118H03: Note 582: the words of Bharadwaja and Bhrigu may refer to a next world, but Bhrigu's answer points to a region on earth, and the reference to Himavat is metaphorical.
shots.B12C362S118H04: Note 583: Nilakantha would read amritya for mritya, a forced correction that keeps the metaphor.
shots.B12C362S118H05: Note 584: all knowledge there is certain.
shots.B12C362S119H01: Note 585: the phrase means practise yoga, and the Bengal reading is dharanam; the commentator reads all the verses as metaphor.
shots.B12C362S119H02: Note 586: this verse plainly refers to the next world, which suggests the whole passage describes it, not an imaginary region north of the Himalayas.
shots.B12C362S119H03: Note 587: Pushkara in Rajputana is said to be the place where Brahman did penance.
shots.B12C362S119H04: Note 588: the Burdwan translator garbles verse 21, which runs into 22, and K.P. Singha avoids the error.
shots.B12C362S119H05: Note 589: the five limbs to be washed before eating are the two feet, the two hands, and the face.
shots.B12C362S120H01: Note 590: this may be a general rule for washing the hand after eating, or the gandusha rite of sipping water.
shots.B12C362S120H02: Note 591: the Burdwan translator has completely misunderstood this verse.
shots.B12C362S120H03: Note 592: the verse is hard, and the commentator reads it as saying such men cannot attain Mahadayu, which is Brahma and not long life.
shots.B12C362S120H04: Note 593: the commentator explains prishtamangsa as meat forming the remnant of a Sraddha offering, which the translator does not find necessary to change.

B12C363.summary: This last section of the chapter has no narrative of its own in this file. It is a run of Ganguli's translator notes, numbered from 594 on, that explain Sanskrit words, variant readings, and the doctrine of Bhishma's teaching on the mind, the soul, yoga, the three qualities, and the illusion of the world. The notes also compare the teaching with Sankhya, Vedanta, Buddhist, and sceptical views of rebirth. They matter as the translator's guide to how the difficult closing doctrine should be read.

scenes.B12C363S254: Notes 1854 to 1858, on sat and asat as effect and cause, honouring Hari and Mantra, the reading gavamritam, rent-free lands for Brahmanas, and Rudra's third eye.
scenes.B12C363S255: Notes 1859 to 1863, on the Manwantara and the Vaivaswat Manu, the powers of yoga, the three currents of the Ganga and Bharadwaja's water, Vishnu's three strides, and the Sreevatsa mark.
scenes.B12C363S256: Notes 1864 to 1868, on Hrishikesa again, the unborn as the eternal soul, the Sattwata race, the five elements mixed in unequal parts, and Achyuta as the unswerving.
scenes.B12C363S257: Notes 1869 to 1873, on clarified butter as the sustainer of the universe, the bodily humours, Narayana in the solar disc, the rarity of devotees, and the branches of the Yajur-Veda.
scenes.B12C363S258: Notes 1874 to 1878, on the Krityas, the path of Dhyana and Galava's race, Narayana's four forms, the grass Munja, and Nara's broken weapon.
scenes.B12C363S259: Notes 1879 to 1883, on the forms of Nara and Narayana, the speaker to Arjuna, Kala as time and death, Arjuna as the ostensible instrument, and who answers Janamejaya.
scenes.B12C363S260: Notes 1884 to 1888, on the word for shoulder joints, the Bengal reading ashta-bhujau, the calm of Nara and Narayana before Narada, the displayed and undisplayed Hari, and Milton's mount of God.
scenes.B12C363S261: Notes 1889 to 1893, on the earth's forbearance, sat and asat as aught and naught, the gods' forgotten Vedas and the teacher as father, the Hari-Gita, and the unclear guru of this verse.
scenes.B12C363S262: Notes 1894 to 1898, on Vasudeva as witness of countless creations, the speech attributed to Saunaka, the horse-headed form, the science of krama, and those who have burnt their fuel.
scenes.B12C363S263: Notes 1899 to 1903, on Vasudeva as the fourth, the ends reached by knowers and devotees, the ekantin as a worshipper without desire, the age without evil, and the Jeshthya Saman.
scenes.B12C363S264: Notes 1904 to 1908, on Ikshaku as progenitor of the solar kings, yoga-kshema and the desire for liberation, the awakened, the rewards of pravritti and nivritti, and the subtle sattwa that frees.
scenes.B12C363S265: Notes 1909 to 1913, on the Ekantins' practices as scriptural, the Whites as householders or the White Island folk, Apantara-tamas, the arrangement of the Vedic hymns, and the sense of twamrite.
scenes.B12C363S266: Notes 1914 to 1918, on thoughts that do not match acts, the word nandana as son and delighter, the single Purusha of highest truth, the feet of the reverend, and the qualities of Purusha.
scenes.B12C363S267: Notes 1919 to 1923, on acts as seeds, three views of the soul, the subtle body and its possessions, Dhaturadyam Vidhanam as Mahat, and the pragvansa part of the altar.
scenes.B12C363S268: Notes 1924 to 1928, on an added passage that explains the connection, Yudhishthira's question on the best mode of life, family custom as binding, the Vedas as unwritten Srutis, and the craving of kankhami and ichcchemi.
scenes.B12C363S269: Notes 1929 to 1933, on sattwika beings, Yama's standards, nityasalila, the uninvited guest who arrives hungry, dwiruna as less than ten by two, and frugality as restraint of the senses.
scenes.B12C363S270: Notes 1934 to 1938, on the Nagas who hear with their eyes, the sense of annyayinah, the Chataka bird and its rain-water, a verse wrongly rendered, and K.P. Singha's close sense.
scenes.B12C363S271: Notes 1939 to 1943, on the phrase we are your slaves, atmanam and atmasthah, the unccha vow of gleaning, diksha as the formal start of sacred acts, and Bhishma's abduction of the Kasi princesses.
scenes.B12C363S272: Project Gutenberg licence text that closes the source file; it is not part of the chapter's own narrative or notes.

shots.B12C363S01H01: Note 594: the sacred thread is wound round the thumb, as the Grihyasutras prescribe.
shots.B12C363S01H02: Note 595: the recipient's formulas of satisfaction, and a note on krisara, a dish of rice and pulses.
shots.B12C363S01H03: Note 596: the polite form of address, bhavan, uses the third person, since the second person is too direct.
shots.B12C363S01H04: Note 597: the recollection of sins makes the sinner miserable, though the text does not say how sins reach him.
shots.B12C363S01H05: Note 598: merit and sin depend on the mind, so even mental harm to others is condemned.
shots.B12C363S02H01: Note 599: if the mind is sinful, no associate can help, since the mind alone is the cause of virtue.
shots.B12C363S02H02: Note 600: adhyatma covers whatever depends on the mind, including the yoga of the mind.
shots.B12C363S02H03: Note 601: the question seems a repetition, but it follows Bhishma's claim that righteousness belongs to the mind.
shots.B12C363S02H04: Note 602: the Sanskrit word vijnanani is better rendered as cognitions.
shots.B12C363S02H05: Note 603: the mind, understanding, and soul are distinguished, with the soul as a portion of the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S03H01: Note 604: Goodness covers high moral qualities, Passion covers love and worldly emotions, and Darkness covers anger and lust.
shots.B12C363S03H02: Note 605: the translator follows Nilakantha's grammar but finds the verse unclear, and asks whether Bhishma teaches idealism.
shots.B12C363S03H03: Note 606: followers of Reid, the note says, treated perceptions as modifications of the mind and denied the outside world.
shots.B12C363S03H04: Note 607: the ocean simile illustrates the rare feat of transcending the three attributes through yoga power.
shots.B12C363S03H05: Note 608: one should trace a harmful thought to its cause, which is Passion, and dispel it.
shots.B12C363S04H01: Note 609: the first two words of the second line repeat verse 5 of the earlier section.
shots.B12C363S04H02: Note 610: Nilakantha explains one word as due to great ill-luck.
shots.B12C363S04H03: Note 611: the translator does not follow Nilakantha in rendering this verse.
shots.B12C363S04H04: Note 612: the soul is a witness, not an actor, and the note compares this to the conscience as an impartial judge.
shots.B12C363S04H05: Note 613: such a person transcends the three qualities, instead of being carried along by them.
shots.B12C363S05H01: Note 614: Nilakantha treats the third line as elliptical and supplies a verb.
shots.B12C363S05H02: Note 615: explains several words, and gives the commentator's view that acts are a hindrance to liberation.
shots.B12C363S05H03: Note 616: explains words for lust and wrath, and says sinful acts bring fear both here and hereafter.
shots.B12C363S05H04: Note 617: Bhishma prefers the yoga that trains mind and understanding to Vedic rites, for quicker liberation.
shots.B12C363S05H05: Note 618: the soul-state is one of purity, lost through worldly attachment and regained by yoga.
shots.B12C363S06H01: Note 619: vichara, viveka, and vitarka are technical terms for stages of progress in yoga.
shots.B12C363S06H02: Note 620: all attainments come from exertion or destiny, and yoga felicity is reached by neither.
shots.B12C363S06H03: Note 621: the commentator takes Sankhya here to mean Vedanta inquiry.
shots.B12C363S06H04: Note 622: according to Sankhya, silent recitation of mantras is not needed, and mental meditation can lead to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S06H05: Note 623: silent recitation of Om may continue only until one sees one's own soul.
shots.B12C363S07H01: Note 624: the two paths are action, called pravritti, and abstention, called nivritti; the first gives rise to sacrifice.
shots.B12C363S07H02: Note 625: one must first cleanse the heart through the virtues already listed.
shots.B12C363S07H03: Note 626: samadhi is meditation with the senses drawn into the mind, fixed on Brahma alone.
shots.B12C363S07H04: Note 627: the goal of yoga is freedom from decay and death, a death at will, or absorption into Brahma.
shots.B12C363S07H05: Note 628: hell here means the opposite of liberation, since heaven still brings rebirth.
shots.B12C363S08H01: Note 629: even this is a kind of hell, since rebirth follows it.
shots.B12C363S08H02: Note 630: godlike powers such as becoming tiny or huge are below the goal of absorption into the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S08H03: Note 631: a faulty line in the Bengal texts is omitted in the Bombay text, which makes verses 10 and 11 couplets.
shots.B12C363S08H04: Note 632: the phrase is explained as giving up enjoyments without really being detached.
shots.B12C363S08H05: Note 633: in that state there are no forms to be objects, so all is pure knowledge.
shots.B12C363S09H01: Note 634: lists the six Angas of the Vedas: pronunciation, ritual, grammar, etymology, metre, and astronomy.
shots.B12C363S09H02: Note 635: an insight gained by intuition and not in the ordinary way.
shots.B12C363S09H03: Note 636: K.P. Singha mistranslates sadhaye, which means I go, and the Burdwan rendering is correct.
shots.B12C363S09H04: Note 637: work and abstention from work are the two courses of duty.
shots.B12C363S09H05: Note 638: Vikrita gave away a cow and transferred the merit of that gift to Virupa.
shots.B12C363S10H01: Note 639: a gleaner picks up single grains from the crevices of harvested fields.
shots.B12C363S10H02: Note 640: Virupa returns the merit of one cow, and Vikrita offers in return the merit of two cows he has given.
shots.B12C363S10H03: Note 641: the king says the dispute has come before him, and he must judge fairly without taking gifts as a Brahmin would.
shots.B12C363S10H04: Note 642: the king feels drawn to accept the gift, but kingly rules restrain him, so he offers his own merit in return.
shots.B12C363S10H05: Note 643: this is not liberation, only terminable felicity.
shots.B12C363S11H01: Note 644: the phrase means attaining emancipation or absorption into the essence of Brahma.
shots.B12C363S11H02: Note 645: the four means of knowledge are direct perception, revelation, inference, and intuition.
shots.B12C363S11H03: Note 646: six states of suffering, hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, disease, and death, and sixteen parts, the breaths, senses, and mind.
shots.B12C363S11H04: Note 647: K.P. Singha misunderstands three ends: absorption, terminable pleasure, and the happiness of freedom from desire.
shots.B12C363S11H05: Note 648: the king asks the Brahmin to share with him the rewards he has won.
shots.B12C363S12H01: Note 649: yogins attain Brahma even in this life, while reciters attain him only after death.
shots.B12C363S12H02: Note 650: the speaker professes to worship a god he does not know, which Vrihaspati calls false, and asks how to be rescued from such falsehood.
shots.B12C363S12H03: Note 651: explains the six Vedangas, covering prosody, astronomy, etymology, rites, and pronunciation.
shots.B12C363S12H04: Note 652: those who think happiness is not eternal drop pious acts and seek knowledge and liberation.
shots.B12C363S12H05: Note 653: the meaning of hell in such passages was explained earlier.
shots.B12C363S13H01: Note 654: Vrihaspati means by acts sacrifices and other observances, which he says are needed to secure the aims of life.
shots.B12C363S13H02: Note 655: one should practise acts as a preparation and then give them up for the higher end, so they help toward Brahma indirectly.
shots.B12C363S13H03: Note 656: mind and acts create all things, and both are good paths if the fruits of acts are mentally abandoned.
shots.B12C363S13H04: Note 657: Nilakantha reads the grammar of the first line differently, and the translator proposes a better construction.
shots.B12C363S13H05: Note 658: acts have three kinds of attributes, good, passionate, and dark, and the mind determines the kind of fruit.
shots.B12C363S14H01: Note 659: this is a cruce, and Nilakantha's reading is correct; the words are taken as unconnected.
shots.B12C363S14H02: Note 660: acts done by the body lead to heaven, while liberation must be sought through the mind.
shots.B12C363S14H03: Note 661: liberation needs freedom from all acts, including recitation and meditation, since these are acts too.
shots.B12C363S14H04: Note 662: the note explains the words as referring to taste and the other senses.
shots.B12C363S14H05: Note 663: existent is the atom, non-existent is space, and existent-and-non-existent is Maya or illusion.
shots.B12C363S15H01: Note 664: the commentator explains the phrase as lacking any notion of a knower.
shots.B12C363S15H02: Note 665: one sees one's own soul.
shots.B12C363S15H03: Note 666: the soul divides into a thousand forms, like the moon's image in agitated water.
shots.B12C363S15H04: Note 667: good and evil fruits dwell together, and knowledge resides in the material body, which is the analogy.
shots.B12C363S15H05: Note 668: the translator cannot see why the image of lamps set on trees is introduced.
shots.B12C363S16H01: Note 669: fire, wind, sunlight, and rivers all return after they seem to die, which shows the body changes form without being destroyed.
shots.B12C363S16H02: Note 670: the soul exists in its own nature, unaffected by qualities and accidents.
shots.B12C363S16H03: Note 671: the correct readings are samanah and sabuddhih, and the Bombay edition has a misprint.
shots.B12C363S16H04: Note 672: the translators misread linga in verses 14 and 15, which here means the gross body.
shots.B12C363S16H05: Note 673: the commentator cites a parallel passage in the Gita about the senses above the body.
shots.B12C363S17H01: Note 674: the verse suggests the Rishis knew spectacles or a microscope, which the commentator calls upanetra.
shots.B12C363S17H02: Note 675: explains the phrase by death on sleep.
shots.B12C363S17H03: Note 676: explains words such as simultaneous and independent, and says a dreaming soul is distinct from senses and body.
shots.B12C363S17H04: Note 677: the soul knows pleasures and pains that arise from the three attributes, but does not enjoy them and is a silent witness.
shots.B12C363S17H05: Note 678: as wind is separate from the fire in a stick, so the soul is separate from the senses.
shots.B12C363S18H01: Note 679: the Bengal reading indriyanam is adopted, and the Bombay reading is set aside.
shots.B12C363S18H02: Note 680: a tree is not before birth and not after destruction, so its form is only an interim state.
shots.B12C363S18H03: Note 681: the translators misrender the second line, and the words jneyam and jnanabhisamhitam name Brahma.
shots.B12C363S18H04: Note 682: tamas is Rahu, and the moon's waxing and waning serves as the simile for the approach of darkness.
shots.B12C363S18H05: Note 683: in dream and deep sleep the subtle form is detached from the body, which shows emancipation is possible.
shots.B12C363S19H01: Note 684: the form caswasasya is explained as naming the main attribute that goes with an object.
shots.B12C363S19H02: Note 685: the word indriyarupani means forms perceived through the senses.
shots.B12C363S19H03: Note 686: the objects to be abandoned are those the senses grasp and the subtle forms of primordial matter.
shots.B12C363S19H04: Note 687: the phrase means that one regains one's real nature.
shots.B12C363S19H05: Note 688: the Bombay reading aptavan is adopted, and pravritti dharma is the religion of action.
shots.B12C363S20H01: Note 689: abstaining from objects conquers desire only in part, and desire is suppressed only when one sees one's soul.
shots.B12C363S20H02: Note 690: the first clause denies an objective world, so objects have only a subjective existence, which the note compares with European views of matter.
shots.B12C363S20H03: Note 691: te is explained as Brahmabhigatah, and K.P. Singha's last foot is wrong.
shots.B12C363S20H04: Note 692: te in the first line means tava, your.
shots.B12C363S20H05: Note 693: the words jnanam and jneyam are used inconsistently in the original.
shots.B12C363S21H01: Note 694: ordinary men treat attributes as separate from substances, but the first step is to see them as one, a view close to European idealism, and then contemplation annihilates attributes to reach Brahma.
shots.B12C363S21H02: Note 695: antaratmanudarsini means that which has the inner self as witness, and the Burdwan rendering of the second line is wrong.
shots.B12C363S21H03: Note 696: the first knowledge is of the true link between soul and not-soul, and fruits are the bodies gained in rebirth.
shots.B12C363S21H04: Note 697: sorrow comes from the relation of knower and known, and whatever depends on that relation is transitory.
shots.B12C363S21H05: Note 698: the translator takes the plain meaning rather than Nilakantha's learned explanation.
shots.B12C363S22H01: Note 699: yogins lured by the wish for extraordinary powers and the bliss of highest heaven do not behold the Supreme.
shots.B12C363S22H02: Note 700: the word gunam means attributes, so the phrase means objects possessed of attributes.
shots.B12C363S22H03: Note 701: the so-called external world has no objective existence, so the mind sees and hears itself.
shots.B12C363S22H04: Note 702: a cruce; the note reads gunadana as the withdrawal of the senses into the mind and then into understanding, which yields the powers of yogins.
shots.B12C363S22H05: Note 703: happiness and sorrow have an end, and the soul will reach its final resting place, which the note links to a doctrine of endless spiritual improvement.
shots.B12C363S23H01: Note 704: rishavam sarvattwam means the bull of the Sattwatas, and here it refers to righteous persons who prize Goodness.
shots.B12C363S23H02: Note 705: Prajapati means lord of creatures, a name for sons of Brahman who begot children.
shots.B12C363S23H03: Note 706: Samavartin is another name for Yama, the punisher of the wicked.
shots.B12C363S23H04: Note 707: nirapekshan is explained as gazing only toward hell, and the Burdwan idea of nomads is unsupported.
shots.B12C363S23H05: Note 708: K.P. Singha takes Naravara as a tribe, which the translator calls a careless blunder.
shots.B12C363S24H01: Note 709: the sandhyakala is the junction of the Treta and Dwapara ages, a time of terrible famine when Viswamitra ate a dog's haunch.
shots.B12C363S24H02: Note 710: the correct reading is mahatmana, which points to Krishna, and the Burdwan translator misrenders it.
shots.B12C363S24H03: Note 711: the verse shows a dispute over Krishna's supremacy, since Sisupala and Jarasandha refused to accept his divinity.
shots.B12C363S24H04: Note 712: the etymology of Sanatana given here is fanciful, since the word normally means eternal.
shots.B12C363S24H05: Note 713: atma atmanah is explained as the true nature of the living soul.
shots.B12C363S25H01: Note 714: the word swamatmanam is explained as the true identity of the self.
shots.B12C363S25H02: Note 715: if all men share one material cause, why do the Srutis and Smritis differ about their duties?
shots.B12C363S25H03: Note 716: at the start of each age the rules of conduct and marriage arise anew, and knowledge of duty grows with the human race until the Creator withdraws all.
shots.B12C363S25H04: Note 717: the word here means the body.
shots.B12C363S25H05: Note 718: a river cannot exist without water, and the soul cannot exist without a body, except when yoga separates them.
shots.B12C363S26H01: Note 719: the mind has no existence apart from the soul, like the second moon seen in water.
shots.B12C363S26H02: Note 720: swabhavahetuja bhava means the virtuous and vicious propensities from past acts, while all else comes from Avidya or Maya.
shots.B12C363S26H03: Note 721: verses 3 and 4 are linked; propensities born of ignorance are the same as the lower propensities, while higher aspirations come from Brahma direct.
shots.B12C363S26H04: Note 722: before creation there was only the soul with knowledge, and its connection with the world is neither necessary nor eternal.
shots.B12C363S26H05: Note 723: the soul's sense that it is a man or an animal is like dreaming that one is a king, and the origin of this delusion cannot be traced.
shots.B12C363S27H01: Note 724: desires lead the soul into a form, acts lead to new desires, and the circle of existence has no beginning or end.
shots.B12C363S27H02: Note 725: the cause is ignorance and the effect is the body and senses, and the acts done through them become causes of new states.
shots.B12C363S27H03: Note 726: as wind stays pure while bearing dust, the soul remains unattached to body and senses.
shots.B12C363S27H04: Note 727: the Vedas urge both action and abstention, action as a step toward abstention, and few understand this.
shots.B12C363S27H05: Note 728: deha-yapanam means severing the body's bond, and acts should be done only to purify, not for the fruit of heaven.
shots.B12C363S28H01: Note 729: vipakram is explained as unripe, and apakvakashayakhya as the teaching given to one whose passions are not matured.
shots.B12C363S28H02: Note 730: anuplavan means following, and akramya means crushing.
shots.B12C363S28H03: Note 731: vijnana here means the loss or absence of knowledge.
shots.B12C363S28H04: Note 732: yathartham means for the true aims of life, acting righteously and gaining liberation.
shots.B12C363S28H05: Note 733: the soul was once pure knowledge, and union with ignorance created the universe, so consciousness is the root of all sorrow.
shots.B12C363S29H01: Note 734: if all rests on consciousness, why are waking perceptions uniform unlike the irregular dreams, and the answer is that past acts produce this uniformity, as time produces the seasons.
shots.B12C363S29H02: Note 735: the last line is expanded to make the sense of nasyati clear, following Nilakantha's simile.
shots.B12C363S29H03: Note 736: the Srutis say Brahma has knowledge, ignorance, and Maya, and it is Maya that binds the living souls to worldly things.
shots.B12C363S29H04: Note 737: mana is worship of one's own self, darpa is freedom from restraint, and ahankara is disregard of others, and ahankara is not consciousness.
shots.B12C363S29H05: Note 738: kritalakshanah is explained as kritaswikarah, meaning that which is accepted or made.
shots.B12C363S30H01: Note 739: Prakriti binds the soul and causes its birth, women are Prakriti and men are souls, so men should avoid women; the note notes the popularity of this doctrine in Indian languages.
shots.B12C363S30H02: Note 740: kritya is the power of Atharvan rites, and women are as dangerous as such rites, sunk so deeply in Rajas as to be invisible.
shots.B12C363S30H03: Note 741: vermin spring from sweat and filth, and children from the seed, so one's offspring are like vermin on the body, and wisdom teaches indifference to both.
shots.B12C363S30H04: Note 742: Rajas causes the impulse to act, Sattwa leads to Brahma, and both rest on Tamas.
shots.B12C363S30H05: Note 743: knowledge overspread by darkness is the seed of the body, and the Burdwan and K.P. Singha versions misread the second line.
shots.B12C363S31H01: Note 744: in the womb the soul remembers past acts, and these shape the senses and the character of the new life.
shots.B12C363S31H02: Note 745: the translator disagrees with Nilakantha's grammar, since tebhyah tyagat is not a violation, and the ablative is not rare here.
shots.B12C363S31H03: Note 746: the senses come from Rajas, so the conquest of Rajas, with sharpened vision from scripture, is needed.
shots.B12C363S31H04: Note 747: the note explains that the two classes of senses, of knowledge and of action, are escaped from rebirth in liberation.
shots.B12C363S31H05: Note 748: arthasamanyam is explained as the highest liberation, and the Pravritti religion cannot reach it, though its followers gain good qualities.
shots.B12C363S32H01: Note 749: the Krichchra vow is a set of fasts, including three days standing in water up to the chin.
shots.B12C363S32H02: Note 750: the three Riks begin with ritam and satyam, and every Brahmin who knows his prayers knows them well.
shots.B12C363S32H03: Note 751: the verse describes yoga, sending the breaths up the Sushumna duct and reducing the attributes to the state beyond the senses.
shots.B12C363S32H04: Note 752: the knowledge beyond the senses is real, and a sage who has it sees the world as mind, and such a mind is eternal, free of passion, and luminous; this is liberation in life.
shots.B12C363S32H05: Note 753: the phrase means freeing oneself from Passion and Darkness by practising abstention from acts.
shots.B12C363S33H01: Note 754: adatte comes from a root meaning to cut, and manasam volam means desires, so a man of ripe understanding gains knowledge that does not decay with age.
shots.B12C363S33H02: Note 755: compassion can lead to excess attachment, as with Bharata and his deer, who was reborn as a deer for thinking of one at death.
shots.B12C363S33H03: Note 756: K.P. Singha translates this verse wrongly, and the Burdwan rendering is correct.
shots.B12C363S33H04: Note 757: the buddhi here is intelligence cleansed by scripture, and samahitam manak means mind freed from anger and malice.
shots.B12C363S33H05: Note 758: one should not covet kingdoms or thrones, and the non-existent objects are sons and wives who are dead, unborn, or unwed.
shots.B12C363S34H01: Note 759: samsara means this world and the next, and words spoken are never destroyed, affecting speaker and listener over countless lives, which the note compares to Babbage's view of indestructible energy.
shots.B12C363S34H02: Note 760: confession of one's acts destroys their effects and stops them recurring.
shots.B12C363S34H03: Note 761: robbers laden with booty are always at risk, and unintelligent men bearing life's burdens are likewise liable to destruction.
shots.B12C363S34H05: Note 763: the reading prakasela is adopted, with Nilakantha's interpretation.
shots.B12C363S35H01: Note 764: kulmasha is ripe grain or seeds, pinyaka is an oil cake of sesame or mustard, and yavaka is unripe barley boiled in hot water.
shots.B12C363S35H02: Note 765: before creation the soul had only knowledge, and ignorance from Brahma made it an ordinary creature, so it took its own products for things independent of itself.
shots.B12C363S35H03: Note 766: the correct reading is upagatasprihah, and the first verse is for yogins, the second for yogins and others alike.
shots.B12C363S35H04: Note 767: dreams come from impressions of this life and of past lives, which the Soul keeps and calls up, a view the note links to Avicenna's theory.
shots.B12C363S35H05: Note 768: one of the three attributes, brought to the mind by past acts, makes the subtle elements produce images that match it.
shots.B12C363S36H01: Note 769: only yoga can destroy these images, since they spring from desires generated by past acts.
shots.B12C363S36H02: Note 770: the Bombay reading Manohrishyan is better.
shots.B12C363S36H03: Note 771: the external and inner worlds both come from consciousness, which comes from delusion affecting the soul, so the soul knowing itself gains omniscience.
shots.B12C363S36H04: Note 772: the body is the door of dreams because it comes from past acts, and in dreamless sleep the senses sink into the mind and the mind into the soul.
shots.B12C363S36H05: Note 773: a purified mind gains omniscience and omnipotence.
shots.B12C363S37H01: Note 774: the Burdwan translator jumbles Nilakantha's gloss and makes nonsense of both text and gloss.
shots.B12C363S37H02: Note 775: Brahma cannot be seized like a creature; it is understood only by reason and analogy, through withdrawal of the senses.
shots.B12C363S37H03: Note 776: the commentator takes the Rishi to be Narayana, friend of Nara, whose retreat at Vadari Vyasa later used.
shots.B12C363S37H04: Note 777: the Pravritti religion of acts cannot free from rebirth, while the Nivritti religion of abstention leads to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S37H05: Note 778: nidarsarkah is explained as wishing to see.
shots.B12C363S38H01: Note 779: the unmanifest is primordial matter, and beyond both matter and Purusha is the Supreme Soul, Brahma.
shots.B12C363S38H02: Note 780: Purusha is non-creating and beyond the three attributes, as the commentator explains.
shots.B12C363S38H03: Note 781: asamhatau means utterly separate, and the two Purushas are the chit-soul and the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S38H04: Note 782: four topics are set out: how Prakriti and Purusha resemble and differ, and how Purusha and Iswara do; the four grounds are no beginning or end, consciousness, distinction, and activity.
shots.B12C363S38H05: Note 783: the note says the common saying about yogins beholding the Lord is the praise of yoga.
shots.B12C363S39H01: Note 784: the commentator says the verse means dying at a sacred place such as Kasi, where Siva himself guides the dying man to liberation.
shots.B12C363S39H02: Note 785: divested of Rajas means freed from the senses and their pleasures.
shots.B12C363S39H03: Note 786: the destruction of the gross body means escape from rebirth, and the karana body is a subtler form than the linga-sarira.
shots.B12C363S39H04: Note 787: when knowledge of Brahma arises, the mistaken who take the body for the self are caught in endless births and deaths without liberation.
shots.B12C363S39H05: Note 788: the commentator takes patience as staying in yoga posture and adoring the senses as Prana and the Indriyas; the translator doubts this leads to Brahma.
shots.B12C363S40H01: Note 789: the stages from the Gita are senses, objects, mind, understanding, soul, Unmanifest, and Purusha, and nothing is above Purusha.
shots.B12C363S40H02: Note 790: a flash of lightning seen again and again becomes a mass of blazing light, which may be the speaker's meaning.
shots.B12C363S40H03: Note 791: the Bengal texts make verse 28 a triplet, and the correct word is dehantam.
shots.B12C363S40H04: Note 792: the three are Mara, meaning the effects, Prakriti, their material cause, and Purusha, the Supreme Soul.
shots.B12C363S40H05: Note 793: another reading names censurers of the various Lokayatika sects.
shots.B12C363S41H01: Note 794: the mind is described as having five currents.
shots.B12C363S41H02: Note 795: the five sheaths are food, breath, mind, knowledge, and bliss, and the note refers the reader to Wilson's dictionary.
shots.B12C363S41H03: Note 796: the verb nyavedayat means started for discourse, and the Burdwan rendering of it is incorrect.
shots.B12C363S41H04: Note 797: the Burdwan version wrongly says Asuri learned from his disciple's questions, while samprishtah means carefully asked.
shots.B12C363S41H05: Note 798: kutumvini means a matron or a householder's wife.
shots.B12C363S42H01: Note 799: the speaker is either Markandeya or Sanatkumara, according to the commentator.
shots.B12C363S42H02: Note 800: the Sankhya view is that every state of life brings sorrow, and the goal of that philosophy is the permanent end of sorrow.
shots.B12C363S42H03: Note 801: these are the marks of the delusion under which man is born and lives until he conquers sorrow.
shots.B12C363S42H04: Note 802: the death of the soul is its extinction, the verse gives the sceptics' opinion, and K.P. Singha's rendering is wrong.
shots.B12C363S42H05: Note 803: this and the following verses are the sceptics' arguments.
shots.B12C363S43H01: Note 804: verse 29 is very terse and lists the heads of sceptical arguments that nothing exists beyond the seen and felt body.
shots.B12C363S43H02: Note 805: the translator uses more words than the Sanskrit, and calls these verses cruces meant to stagger Ganesa.
shots.B12C363S43H03: Note 806: the commentator calls the rebirth theory in verse 34 Buddhist, and verse 35 refutes it, since Buddhists deny an indestructible soul.
shots.B12C363S43H04: Note 807: the acts of one person do not affect another, so no proof exists that acts in one life carry over to a different being, using the example of Chaitra and Maitra.
shots.B12C363S43H05: Note 808: the translator's literal rendering of the second line would be unintelligible, so a fuller version is given.
shots.B12C363S44H01: Note 809: if Consciousness is destroyed and reborn, Buddhist Nirvana cannot be the final liberation of the Brahmanical texts.
shots.B12C363S44H02: Note 810: the Buddhists gain nothing by a permanent soul, since the Brahmanical soul has no attributes and a soul with attributes would be destructible.
shots.B12C363S44H03: Note 811: the senses merge into their causes, and the speaker argues that a substance also perishes with its attributes, so the analogy fails.
shots.B12C363S44H04: Note 812: here the speaker attacks the orthodox Brahmanical doctrine of the soul.
shots.B12C363S44H05: Note 813: this is perhaps because such doctrines are based on Revelation.
